extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history; art historians, critics, and sculptors interested in ancient Greek sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and standards used in an art-historical essay for judging early Greek sculpture — technical execution, material choices, stylistic individuality, religious function, and aesthetic ideals. Useful for assessing or producing works in the archaic-to-classical Greek sculptural tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth in organic form / freedom of movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek art is essentially distinguished by an "energetic striving after truth in organic form"; the Greek apprehends the human figure as a living organism with freedom of movement, and hence the infinite possibilities of motion and of expression by motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate figures for natural anatomy, suggestive ability to move, openness of eyes, separation of feet, and other signs that a statue 'seems to walk' or 'seems to look'. Contrast with purely mathematical or mechanical proportions (Egyptian art). Emphasis is on vitality and believable potential motion rather than static formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of human soul / inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of the Greek sculptor, together with its more real anatomy, becomes full also of human soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the sculpture communicates inner spirit or personality — not merely physical likeness but emotion, dignity, or solemnity. Look for expression in posture, gesture, and facial composition that conveys an inward life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious consecration and hieratic/sacred quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Early images underwent consecration at their first erecting and were conceived as the actual dwelling-place of a god; sculptural production was a religious enthusiasm with a hieratic or sacred quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For temple or cult images, consider evidence of ritual function, consecration, and hieratic composure. The degree of 'piety' or religious temperament in conception and treatment can be a criterion of authenticity and intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of individual personality / master's style
rubrics_metrics.description: The development of the artist out of the mere craftsman leads to real personalities with individual characteristics: temperament, talent, motives, and what we call style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works for signs of personal invention — resemblances amid differences between pieces that indicate a single hand or 'style of a master' rather than uniform workshop manufacture. Consider innovations, idiosyncratic motifs, and distinguishing executional marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material-driven modification and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Material (ivory and gold, bronze, cedar-wood, marble) influences conception and execution — 'the likeness between two statues is not the mechanical likeness... but with modifications ... due to the difference of the material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how choice of material affects scale, surface treatment, balance, and detail. Assess whether the artist used material advantages (e.g., bronze's lightness for tenuity; chryselephantine for richness) to appropriate ends rather than forcing an ill-suited effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic feeling and symbolic conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture may embody poetic motives and symbolic conceptions (e.g., Muse with the Lyre symbolising chromatic music, chryselephantine Aphrodite with attributes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for works intended as poetic or symbolic statements rather than literal portraiture — attributes, gestures, and iconography that communicate higher-order meanings (music, seasons, divine attributes). Value such works for conception and imaginative expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance/harmonisation of Ionian (sensuous) and Dorian (ideal) tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek sculpture harmonises two opposing influences — the Ionian (chryselephantine, sensuous, Asiatic, centrifugal) and the Dorian/European (severe simplification, order, centripetal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a work's success by how well it reconciles sensuous material delight with inward, rational form and proportion. Excess in either variegation/ornament or abstract severity is treated as weakness; best works reflect both craft and intellectual order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of humanity, proportion, and inward harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim is the impression of an order, a sanity, a proportion in all work which shall reflect the inward order of human reason — to express both the indwelling spirit of human intelligence and great human passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proportion, composure, and whether passions and calm are integrated — the body as a language of the soul. Consider if the artist analyses and recomposes bodily elements to convey character and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical composition and engineering (weight, supports, chiselling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical excellence: 'delicate calculation of weight in the composition of the several parts, allowing the artist to dispense with all artificial supports' and the 'bold use of the chisel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge sculptures by structural ingenuity (how weight and balance are achieved), minimal use of supports, daring thinness (e.g., shields, arms), and confident toolwork. Technical solutions that enable complex, free poses are marks of mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finishing and conscientious execution (even in invisible parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fineness of execution 'even in parts of the work invisible to an ordinary spectator,' finished in diligence to satisfy the artist's own conviction of good sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the thoroughness of finishing, attention to hidden surfaces and internal details — evidence of an artist's conviction and care beyond mere public display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration approach: antiquarian vs aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Two legitimate motives in restoration: the antiquarian (present only what actually remains) and the aesthetic (restore with least addition so the object may please the living eye).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restoring or judging restorations, decide whether priority is faithful presentation of surviving fragments or an aesthetic completion for contemporary viewers. Evaluate any restoration on transparency of interventions and fidelity to original design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nude human form as an element of Hellenic temperance and value
rubrics_metrics.description: The more truly Hellenic art adopts the unveiled and healthy human form; undraped figure is an embodiment of the Hellenic spirit and an element of temperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider nudity's symbolic and aesthetic role — as idealisation and temperate expression — and judge whether clothed or unclothed treatment is appropriate to the work's purpose and spirit. Note exceptions (e.g., Paris) and local conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate, limited, and conventional use of color on marble
rubrics_metrics.description: Though marble is the chosen material, traces of colour exist; there was a 'limited and conventionalised use of colour' (shields blue, helmet crests red, eyes and lips coloured).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess painted elements for conventional application that complements form rather than overwhelming it. Recognise that original polychromy was often restrained and symbolic rather than fully naturalistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of mixed media/accessories (metal attachments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marble figures were often combined with metal accessories — holes bored for attachment of lances, swords, bows, and gilt metal details like the Medusa's head — adding refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence of original mixed-media composition and how attachments contributed to overall effect. Presence of metal accessories can indicate technical sophistication and subtler visual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos and humanity versus hardness/cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: True Hellenic art shows pathos and humanity; by contrast, Asiatic/Oriental reliefs often display 'hardness and cruelty' and lack of special humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work evokes pity, tenderness, or humane feeling (pathos) rather than mechanical or brutal depiction. Emotional resonance and humane interest are positive criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle workmanship and inventive devices (mechanical detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtlety of workmanship (e.g., Pliny's account of an automaton stag) hints at the technical sophistication of the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value ingenuity and mechanical invention in a work when appropriate — automata, moving elements, or ingenious fittings are evidence of refined workmanship and inventive talent.
